The name is First Times, Your Rules, with a neon scrapbook look, handheld photos, and copy that treats curiosity as part of becoming independent. The slogan is Try the story, own the choice. The campaign can open with five posts: One: Everyone has a first time for something. Make yours a choice, not a dare. Two: If the group needs you to prove yourself, the group is selling you something. Three: A night you remember is a night you get to tell in your own words. Four: Chemistry, attraction, and peer pressure can all feel thrilling; decide which one is actually driving you. Five: There is no prize for going further than you wanted. The creator talking point is that experimentation is not a moral failure and that young adults should be able to talk about it without being shamed. A creator could say, We grew up hearing either do everything or do nothing. Real life is messier, and the decision belongs to the person living it. To keep the tone from becoming a lecture, the campaign uses first-person stories, playful polls, and visual contrasts between the expectation of an unforgettable night and the awkward reality of being unsure. A launch event could invite readers to submit anonymous first-choice stories, pair a music set with a quiet decompression space, and distribute cards with a ride-home number and sexual-health resources. Every post can include a small reminder that consent must be clear and ongoing, that an intoxicated person cannot consent, and that mixing substances or accepting an unknown substance can be dangerous. Moderators should remove comments that pressure anyone to participate or provide instructions for obtaining drugs. The campaign is deliberately more seductive than a standard warning, because it acknowledges the social rewards that make risky behavior attractive while trying to place choice and boundaries inside the story rather than outside it.

The visual brief should feel intimate and aspirational without showing consumption, intoxication, coercion, or sexual acts. Each post should carry a compact reminder that consent is ongoing and impossible when someone is intoxicated, unknown substances carry serious risks, and anyone can leave. Moderators remove sourcing offers, dares, pressure, and comments aimed at younger readers.
